## The baseline[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/baseline.html#the-baseline)

This page explains the baseline `run` takes before the first hop. Next: [A smoke test for WSU apps](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/smoke-test.html).

Before the first hop, `run` runs the app's own tests (or the built-in `php -l` syntax check when the app has no tests) on the PHP the app is on now, in the same `booster-target:<php>` image the gate uses. The point is to tell "Booster broke it" from "it was already broken": a red baseline means the suite was red before any change, so a later red gate is not proof of a bad hop. The baseline is recorded in the report (`passed`, `failed` or `skipped`, with the exit code and the last 20 lines of output).

- A red baseline stops the run before the first hop, with a non-zero exit. `--allow-failing-baseline` lets it go on; each later gate failure is then labeled "the baseline was already failing" in the text and JSON output.
- `--skip-gate` and `--dry-run` skip the baseline (reported as `skipped`), so a dry run never starts Docker.
- A Mix app's `public/mix-manifest.json` is a build artifact, not committed source: a fresh clone has no manifest, so the suite can be red before any hop. Build the assets before the baseline (the app's usual `npm ci && npm run build`), or pass `--allow-failing-baseline` knowing why.
- When the app has no tests of its own, the baseline and every gate run a built-in check instead: every PHP file outside `vendor/` and `node_modules/` must still parse on the target PHP (`php -l`). That proves the code loads on the new PHP, not that it works: click through the app before you ship. Pass `--test-command` to run something else, or add a smoke test ([A smoke test for WSU apps](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/smoke-test.html)) to get the real gate back.

---

Source: https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/behaviour-changes.html

## Behavior changes[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/behaviour-changes.html#behavior-changes)

This page explains the behavior-change blocks `plan` and `run` print, one per PHP and Laravel hop. Next: [The baseline](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/baseline.html).

Some changes between versions do not raise an error: a function that still exists now means something else, a config key that was optional is required, a default that flipped. Rector rewrites what it knows; the silent changes need a human eye. So `plan` and `run` carry a curated list of them, one block per PHP and Laravel hop, plus the package rows on the last step, where the lock lands. A booster should know its own payload.

```
Behavior changes to check:
  Config key needed (config/app.php)
    check: Add the key.
  Minimum PHP raised
    check: Check the runtime.
```

Each entry says what changed (`label`), what keeps the old behavior when there is anything (`keep old:`), what to verify (`check:`), and where the app touches it: `file:line` hits for code, the file for config and package rows, no location for rows that apply everywhere. It is advisory, like the scans: it never changes the exit code, and nothing prints when nothing matches. In JSON output the entries land under `behaviour_changes`, per step, with the fields `id`, `label`, `keep_old`, `check`, `source`, `hits` and `total`.

An entry may also carry an optional `parity` object: one observable thing, how to read it before the hop, what it must equal after, and how to measure it. When a matched entry has one, the block gains a `Parity checks` section under the same step, one `[ ]` row per entry, so you can write down the before value now and compare it after the hop. The field is optional; entries without it print exactly as before.

```json
{
  "parity": {
    "what": "How long a flashed toast stays open",
    "before": "The timer value the app sets today (SWEET_ALERT_TIMER in .env or 'timer' in config/sweetalert.php)",
    "after": "SWEET_ALERT_TOAST_AUTO_CLOSE (or 'toast.auto_close') must equal that value",
    "how": "Fire a toast and time it with a stopwatch"
  }
}
```

The list lives in `data/behaviour-changes.json`, bundled with the phar. An entry names the hop it applies to (`php-80-to-81`, `laravel-10-to-11`, or `package:vendor/name@2` for a floor a package raises), how to find it (`detect`: a `function`, `method`, `class`, `property`, string `token`, blade snippet, config `file` and `key`, composer `package`, or `always`), and a `source` link that confirms the change:

```json
{
  "id": "laravel-11-config-key",
  "hop": "laravel-10-to-11",
  "detect": { "kind": "config", "file": "config/app.php", "key": "cipher" },
  "label": "Config key needed",
  "keep_old": null,
  "check": "Add the key.",
  "source": "https://laravel.com/docs/11.x/upgrading"
}
```

Only confirmed changes ship, each with its source link, and at most three `always` rows per release, so the block stays a checklist rather than a pamphlet. To add an entry, append it to the data file and let the loader's errors tell you what is missing.

---

Source: https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/citadel.html

## Deploying on Citadel[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/citadel.html#deploying-on-citadel)

This page covers the deployment script Booster writes for a real run. Next: [Checks](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/checks.html).

When a real (not dry) run changes `composer.lock` and the app has a `deployments/` directory, Booster writes one deployment script, `deployments/0000_composer_install_<YYYYMMDDHHMM>`:

```sh
#!/bin/sh
# Added by Booster: this upgrade changed composer.lock. Citadel runs each deployment script once, in name order,
# so a new name makes existing deployments install the new vendor/ before anything else runs.
set -e
composer install --no-dev --no-interaction --optimize-autoloader
php artisan migrate --force
```

Citadel runs every `deployments/` script exactly once, in name order, and the leading `0000` puts this one first. So when the app next deploys, every existing deployment installs the upgraded `vendor/` before any other script runs. The `php artisan migrate --force` line appears only for apps that have an `artisan` file; raw PHP apps get the `composer install` alone. Commit the script with the rest of the upgrade. To drop it again, delete the named file.

---

Source: https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/dependency-check.html

## The dependency check[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/dependency-check.html#the-dependency-check)

This page explains the Packagist check Booster runs before the hops print. Next: [Behavior changes](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/behaviour-changes.html).

Before the hops print, `plan` (and `run`) asks Packagist about each direct third-party dependency in the app's `composer.json`: what is its newest stable release, and can that release still be installed at each hop's destination? Only plain `require` and `require-dev` entries count; PHP, extensions (`ext-*`, `lib-*`), Laravel itself (`laravel/framework`, its `illuminate/*` components) and PHPUnit are Booster's own business, so they are skipped.

The answer is advisory, like the scans: a package that cannot follow the plan does not drop the hop. It adds a warning that names the package, the hop it blocks, and what to do about it:

```
acme/legacy-auth 2.3.0 supports Laravel up to 10 and PHP up to 8.3, so it blocks laravel-10-to-11. Replace or upgrade it first.
```

The warning names only the dimensions the blocked hop fails on: a Laravel ceiling alone, a PHP ceiling alone, or both together. A ceiling is printed as the newest version Booster plans that the constraint allows (a PHP constraint capping at 7.x reads "7.4", not "7"), and a constraint with no upper bound has no ceiling to name, so the warning names its floor instead (`needs PHP 8.2 or newer`).

A package whose newest release requires several `illuminate/*` components is judged by the loosest of those constraints, the one that allows the most Laravel versions. Abandoned packages get their own warning (`acme/old is abandoned (use acme/new instead).`). Packages the check cannot reach are reported as `Not checked: <package> (not on Packagist or unreachable).` or `(VCS repository).`, and the plan goes on. In JSON output every package lands under `package_checks`, with the fields `package`, `newest`, `blocks`, `abandoned` and `checked`.

The check fetches from `repo.packagist.org` and from any composer-type repository the app declares in `composer.json`; VCS repositories are never fetched. `--no-package-check` skips the whole check, for offline use.

---

Source: https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/framework-hops.html

## Hand-copied libraries to Composer[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/framework-hops.html#hand-copied-libraries-to-composer)

This page covers the first framework hop, `vendored-to-composer`: what it moves, what it writes, what makes it refuse, and how the replay gate proves the app still answers the same. Before this: [The replay gate](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/replay-gate.html). Next: [Laravel hops and vendor/](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/laravel-and-vendor.html).

Some apps never met Composer. In 2012 a real WSU app copied Doctrine 2.2, Smarty 3.1 and Slim 1.6 straight into `vendor/`, loaded them with `require` lines, and ran happily until PHP moved on. The PHP hops cannot help it: Booster never edits a library's files, and a 2012 copy of Doctrine crashes on PHP 7.4 before the app's own code runs. So this hop moves the app instead. The hand copies leave, `composer.json` asks for the maintained release of the same library, and the lines that loaded the copies load Composer's autoloader. Every other hop lifts the engine; this one finally gets the parts from a dealer instead of the junkyard.

### In two commands[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/framework-hops.html#in-two-commands)

```sh
booster plan --path=<app> --from-php=5.6 --vendored          # where the move fits, or the stop signs that block it
booster run --path=<app> --from-php=5.6 --vendored --replay  # move it, with the replay as proof
```

Without `--vendored` the plan still finds the copies and says so:

```
The app hand-copied Doctrine, Slim and Smarty into vendor/. Add --vendored to plan the move to Composer.
```

Draft the replay file first (`booster replay init`, see [The replay gate](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/replay-gate.html)). The drafter reads Slim 1 routes (`$app->get('/batches/:id', ...)`), so an old Slim app gets a useful first draft.

### The recipes[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/framework-hops.html#the-recipes)

Each recipe goes to the nearest maintained release that keeps the API the app already calls, so the app's own code does not change. Booster checked these against Packagist on 2026-11-06.

| Copy under `vendor/` | Moves to | Needs PHP | The app's code |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Doctrine 2.x (`vendor/Doctrine`) | `doctrine/orm ^2.20`, `doctrine/annotations ^1.14`, `symfony/cache` | 7.1 | unchanged: ORM 2.20 still has `Setup`, `EntityManager::create()` and docblock annotations |
| Smarty 3.x (`vendor/Smarty`) | `smarty/smarty ^4.5` | 7.1 | unchanged: Smarty 4 keeps the `Smarty` class and its API |
| Slim 1.x (`vendor/Slim`) | `slim/slim ^4.15`, `slim/psr7 ^1.6`, plus `slim1-bridge.php` | 7.4 | unchanged: the bridge keeps `new Slim()`, `$app->get()`, `render()`, `redirect()` and friends |

The planner puts the hop at the first PHP every recipe's release runs on: right after the PHP hop that lands on 7.4 when the app has Slim 1, on 7.1 when it has only Doctrine and Smarty, and first when the app is already there. A plan that ends below that leaves the hop out with a warning.

### What the hop changes[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/framework-hops.html#what-the-hop-changes)

- Deletes each moved copy (`vendor/Doctrine/`, `vendor/Smarty/`, `vendor/Slim/`), and `vendor/` itself when nothing else is left in it. That is the only thing it does to `vendor/`: it never edits a library file.
- Writes `composer.json` (or adds to the app's own): the packages above, `php` at the hop's PHP when the app named none, and `autoload.classmap` for the bridge. A package the app already requires keeps its constraint.
- In each app file, the first `require` or `include` of a moved copy becomes `require_once` of `vendor/autoload.php` with the same path prefix, so `dirname(__FILE__) . '/../vendor/Smarty/Smarty.class.php'` becomes `dirname(__FILE__) . '/../vendor/autoload.php'`. Later requires of the copies go, and so do the 2012 bootstrap lines that pointed at them: `Setup::registerAutoloadDirectory(...)`, `define('SMARTY_DIR', ...)` and `require SMARTY_DIR . 'Smarty.class.php'`. Line endings stay as they were.
- For Slim 1, writes `slim1-bridge.php` at the app root (next section).

The gate then runs `composer install` on the hop's PHP inside the target image, which resolves the packages and writes the app's first `composer.lock`; an app that already had a lock gets `composer update -W` for the new packages only. Then it runs the app's tests, or the syntax check for an app with none, and the replay.

### The Slim 1 bridge[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/framework-hops.html#the-slim-1-bridge)

Slim 4 is not Slim 1: different classes, PSR-7 requests, a different router. Rewriting every route by hand is how a framework move eats a semester. Instead the hop writes `slim1-bridge.php`, about 1,200 lines ported from Slim 1.6.7 (MIT), that keeps Slim 1's classes and behavior and hands the routing and the sending to Slim 4:

- `:param` patterns and conditions, the first registered route wins, parameters url-decoded once and passed in pattern order, echoed output as the body, `Content-Type: text/html` by default;
- the 404, 405 (with `Allow`) and 500 pages byte for byte, the 301 to a trailing slash, `_METHOD` and `X-HTTP-Method-Override`;
- `render()` through the app's own `Slim_View` subclass, `halt()`, `stop()`, `redirect()`, `notFound()`, `error()`, `urlFor()`, `getMode()`, `configureMode()`, route middleware, and the app's own properties on `$app`.

It does not turn a PHP notice into an error page the way Slim 1 did in development mode: on a new PHP every deprecation would become a 500, which is a strange way to celebrate an upgrade. The bridge is the app's code from then on. Move one route at a time to plain Slim 4 (or to Laravel) with the replay green after each, and delete the file when nothing calls `new Slim()` any more.

### Stop signs[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/framework-hops.html#stop-signs)

The hop rewrites a few exact line shapes and nothing else. Anything that touches a moved library in another way is a stop sign: the plan leaves the hop out and names the file and line, and a run that finds one refuses the step and changes nothing.

- Doctrine's own `ClassLoader` (ORM 2.20 no longer ships it; move the app's own classes to Composer's autoload first), or a `registerAutoloadDirectory` call spread over several lines.
- `SMARTY_DIR` used for anything but loading Smarty, or a path into a copy that is not a one-line `require`.
- The Slim 1 API the bridge does not carry: hooks, application middleware (`Slim_Middleware`), `flash()`, cookies through the app or the response, `etag()`, `lastModified()`, `expires()`, `pass()`, `Slim::getInstance()`, and a route pattern with regular-expression characters, which Slim 4's router reads differently.
- A copy whose major the recipe does not cover (Smarty 2, Doctrine 1, Slim 2), an existing `slim1-bridge.php`, or a `composer.json` that is not valid JSON.

A commented-out call is not a stop sign. Booster reads the line, not the vibe.

### What stays[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/framework-hops.html#what-stays)

- Libraries without a recipe (PHPMailer, Swift Mailer, Twig, Monolog, anything Booster does not recognize) stay where they are, still loaded the way they always were, and the hop lists each one as a MANUAL line.
- Copies in a nested `vendor/` (say `admin/vendor/Smarty`) stay too: `composer.json` goes at the app root, so only the root's `vendor/` can be pointed at Composer.

### Why the replay waits[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/framework-hops.html#why-the-replay-waits)

With `--replay`, the baseline is recorded on the app's current PHP as always. The PHP hops before `vendored-to-composer` still run their test gate, but their replay is deferred, because the app still loads its 2012 copies and those may not run on the new PHP; that is the problem the hop exists to fix. From the hop on, every step is compared against the baseline:

```
Replay deferred to step 6 (vendored-to-composer): the app still loads its hand-copied libraries, which may not run on PHP 7.4. The answers are compared once Composer's releases are in.
```

A real app's replay found two Doctrine changes no test asked about: `DISTINCT(alias.field)` in DQL reads as an expression in ORM 2.20, and an entity whose id holds a date needs a custom column type. The hop lists both as MANUAL lines, so you know where to look when the replay says an answer changed.

### After the hop[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/framework-hops.html#after-the-hop)

- Commit `composer.json`, `composer.lock` and, for Slim, `slim1-bridge.php`. Citadel never runs `composer install`, so commit `vendor/` on the deploy branch or let Booster's `deployments/` script install it (see [Deploying on Citadel](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/citadel.html)).
- ORM 2.20 is the last line that reads docblock annotations, and `doctrine/annotations` 1.x is abandoned. ORM 3 (PHP 8.1 or newer, attributes instead of annotations) is the next move, by hand for now. Smarty 5 likewise, once the templates stop using PHP functions as modifiers.
- The lock was resolved on the hop's PHP. Later PHP hops keep it, so run `composer update` once the app lands on its target to pick up the newest releases that PHP allows.

---

Source: https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/hops.html

## What a hop does[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/hops.html#what-a-hop-does)

This page walks through one hop step by step. The full list of hops is in [the reference](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/hops.html).

On PHP hops a pre-pass runs first: PHP 4 era `$a = &new Foo();` becomes a plain assignment, because PHP 7 and newer refuse to compile the old spelling and Rector would never get a parse tree. The report lists the rewrites per file under `Pre-pass fixes:`.

1. Rector runs as a dry run. If it reports errors, the run stops before anything is written. So does a hop that would change more than 200 files, unless an interactive run confirms it after showing the per-rule summary; an explicit `--max-changes` is a hard limit that never asks. An empty Rector report usually means the process ran out of memory, and the message points at `--memory-limit`.
2. Rector runs for real, with only that hop's rules. A rule that would change what the code does is never applied: the PHP 8.0 set's switch-to-match rewrite is skipped, because `match` compares strictly and would stop a `case 1:` from matching the string `"1"` a query string carries. Every run keeps Rector's and PHPStan's caches in its own temp directory, removed at exit, so one run never reads another's.
3. `composer.json` is edited: the `php` or `laravel/framework` constraint is raised, and `config.platform.php` moves with it when the app already pins it, to the first released patch of the new PHP (8.4.1 for 8.4, because 8.4.0 never shipped; x.y.0 otherwise). Booster never creates that key.
4. The gate runs the app's tests inside `booster-target:<php>-<stamp>`, a container built from `docker/Dockerfile` on the PHP the hop moves to. The stamp is a short hash of the recipe, so an edited `docker/Dockerfile` rebuilds the image instead of reusing a stale one. The image carries the extension set Citadel's apps run with: intl, ldap, soap, zip, gd, pdo_mysql, mysqli, bcmath, pcntl, exif, redis, imagick and oci8. The first build downloads Oracle Instant Client for oci8, so it takes a few minutes; later hops reuse the image. Pass `--image` to run the gate in your own image instead (below). A red gate stops the run and leaves the changes in place so you can read them (`git checkout .` undoes them). With `--replay`, the gate also replays the requests recorded before the first hop and fails on a changed answer: see [The replay gate](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/replay-gate.html). To check the image itself, `scripts/check-target-image.sh` (or its Windows twin `check-target-image.ps1`) builds it for each PHP version and verifies its extension list; it needs Docker and a few minutes per version, so it is not part of `composer ci`.
5. On Laravel and PHPUnit hops the gate refreshes the lock before the tests: `composer update -W` for the package the hop moved, so `composer.lock` lands on the new major version next to `composer.json`. A PHP hop on an app that pins `config.platform.php` (every Sourdough app does) runs `composer update --lock`: no package moves, but the lock's `platform-overrides` catch up with the new pin, which a plain `composer install` would otherwise check the raised `php` constraint against and refuse. Every other hop, and the baseline, run a plain `composer install`. The two phases report separately: a Composer failure names the Composer phase and Composer's own output, because the tests never ran.

Composer 2.10 refuses to load tagged releases Packagist has flagged with a security advisory, and hops that move onto Laravel 9 or 10 most often meet that block. The refusal has two faces. The loud one fails the install phase and names the advisories. The quiet one happens when the app allows dev stability: Composer does not fail at all, it locks the branch instead, `9.x-dev` where the hop asks for `^9.0`. Booster reads the refreshed lock back and treats a branch version behind a tagged range like the block. Either way it writes a temporary entry to `config.policy.advisories.ignore` in `composer.json`: scoped to the package and the constraint Composer refused, kept visible to `composer audit`, and carrying a reason PROCTOR can find and report until the app removes it. The gate then retries once. If the retry still fails, the run stops with the unblock and the failure both in the report, and the entry stays in `composer.json`.

The unblock is temporary by name, and Booster enforces that. When a gated step passes, Booster re-reads `config.policy.advisories.ignore` and reports every entry whose reason carries its own prefix (`Booster temporary unblock`; older runs wrote `BOOSTER temporary unblock`, which it still recognizes). A step that is not the plan's last one applies with a warning; the plan's last step fails until the entry is out of `composer.json`, so the final target never ships with the unblock still in place. Removing the entry is the app's job once it is off the blocked versions.

The `--image` value names the image the baseline and every gate run in, and it takes three shapes:

- One name, used for the baseline and every gate: `--image myapp/gate:8.4`.
- A template whose `{php}` is replaced with the PHP version of that baseline or gate: `--image registry/php-apache:{php}` gates the 8.1 hop on `registry/php-apache:8.1` and the 8.2 hop on `registry/php-apache:8.2`.
- A map of PHP version to image, for a fleet whose images do not follow one pattern: `--image 8.0=legacy/php:7.4,8.1=registry/php-apache:8.1`. A map without the version a baseline or hop lands on stops the run before the first hop and names the fix; a template never misses.

Booster never builds a `--image` image: it must exist locally or be pullable, and each resolved image is pulled at most once per run. On an arm64 Mac, Citadel's published images such as `citadel/php-apache:8.5r3` are amd64 only: pass an arm64 build via `--image`, or set `DOCKER_DEFAULT_PLATFORM=linux/amd64` and let Docker emulate. `booster-target` itself builds natively on arm64. And the old-PHP images (5.5 through 8.0) point apt at archive.debian.org, so they get no security updates: they exist to run the app's tests on the way up, not to serve traffic.

`run` refuses to start on a working copy that is not under git or has uncommitted changes, so the upgrade diff stands alone. `--dry-run` has no such limit.

A dry run previews every hop against the original tree, so the same file can appear in several hops. The report ends with the number of unique files and a reminder that nothing was applied. A Laravel hop whose app has no `vendor/` cannot see the framework's classes, so its preview is marked incomplete and the report says to run `composer install` first.

A run prints one line per hop to standard error while it works: the hop's position in the plan, its id, its status, the number of files it changed and the seconds it took, and a final line totals the hops run, the stops and the whole run. They go to standard error so the report on standard output is untouched and `--format json` stays valid JSON.

Four hops edit manifests instead of code. `node-pin-24` sets `engines.node` in `package.json` and writes `.nvmrc`, then the app's usual gate applies. `mix-to-vite` converts a simple `webpack.mix.js` to Vite (see [the hop list](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/hops.html)) and asks for a build gate, which runs `npm ci` and `npm run build` in the `node:26` container before the app's tests. `vite-major` moves a Vite front end onto the Vite major in the hop data: it pins `vite` wherever it sits in `package.json`, pins `laravel-vite-plugin` and `@vitejs/plugin-vue` to the hop data's versions when they are already listed, runs `npm install` in the Node container and asks for a build gate. `tailwind-3-to-4` runs the official `@tailwindcss/upgrade` tool (one exact release, with `--force`) in the Node container, then pins `tailwindcss` to `^4.1`, adds the matching Vite or PostCSS plugin, removes `autoprefixer` and `postcss-import`, which Tailwind 4 folds in, moves an inline `css.postcss` Tailwind block in `vite.config` to the `@tailwindcss/vite` plugin (the early 2025 Laravel starter kit shape; any other config that still imports them gets a MANUAL line), and runs `npm install` so the lock matches; plugins listed in `tailwind.config.js` and `@apply` inside Vue SFC `<style>` blocks stay manual work, and the hop says so. `inertia-2-to-3` raises `inertiajs/inertia-laravel` and `@inertiajs/vue3` to `^3.0` when the plan lands on Laravel 11 or newer on PHP 8.2 or newer, runs `composer update` and `npm install`, and lists the v3 breaking changes as manual lines, because a person works them. `typescript-major` pins `typescript` to `^6.0` wherever it sits in `package.json`, and `vue-tsc` to `^3.0` when the app lists it, runs `npm install` so the lock matches, then asks for the same build gate; when that install has to override a peer dependency, the hop names the package to raise, because the next plain `npm install` would refuse the tree; running the type check and fixing what the new major flags stay manual work, and the hop says so.

Vue 2 to Vue 3 is staged. `vue-26-to-27` moves the front end to the last Vue 2 release, which carries the Vue 3 reactivity API; `vue-27-to-compat` switches to the `@vue/compat` build; `vue-compat-codemod` runs the `vue-upgrade-tool` codemod and keeps every manual item it lists. `vue-2-to-3` is the playbook that stands in for all three: skipping it skips them, and a person finishes the job, because Rector does not read Vue.

---

Source: https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/laravel-and-vendor.html

## Laravel hops and vendor/[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/laravel-and-vendor.html#laravel-hops-and-vendor)

This page covers what Laravel hops need from the app, and where the hop data comes from. Next: [Deploying on Citadel](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/citadel.html).

rector-laravel needs Laravel's classes to recognize a model or a controller. For a Laravel hop Booster loads the app's own `vendor/autoload.php` when it exists, so run `composer install` in the app first. PHP hops never load the app's autoloader. An app with no `vendor/` still gets a plan and the hops that do not need Laravel's classes.

For an Inertia/Vue app, each Laravel hop also raises the Inertia constraints the app already carries: `inertiajs/inertia-laravel` and `@inertiajs/vue3` move to the constraint the hop data pairs with the target major (`^2.0` for Laravel 11 and newer). Booster never adds a package the app does not have, and below Laravel 11 it pins nothing and says so, because the hop data carries no constraint there.

### Hop data[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/laravel-and-vendor.html#hop-data)

`data/versions.json` holds the version facts Booster plans against: the PHP, Laravel and PHPUnit chains, the PHP range each Laravel major supports, the PHPUnit floor each Laravel major ships, the Node floor the `node-pin-24` hop writes, the Vite major and plugin pins the `vite-major` hop uses, and the fixed Tailwind, TypeScript and vue-tsc pins, the fixed Inertia 3 constraints and the Inertia constraint tables the front-end hops use. The file ships inside the PHAR. A new major appears in the file as soon as its feed says so; Booster offers a hop for it only once Rector ships a ruleset for it, and a plan toward a major without one stops there with a warning instead of failing.

`bin/refresh-hop-data.php` rewrites the file from the public feeds (Packagist for PHPUnit and Laravel, endoflife.date for Laravel's supported PHP ranges, npm for the Vite packages) plus CREED's policy for what counts as supported:

```
php bin/refresh-hop-data.php             # fetch the feeds, rewrite the file, print what changed
php bin/refresh-hop-data.php --check     # offline CI check: validate the shape, then compare the frozen feeds
php bin/refresh-hop-data.php --online    # compare against the live feeds without writing the file
php bin/refresh-hop-data.php --offline tests/fixtures/hop-feeds --today 2026-10-29 --dry-run
```

The refresh is deterministic for a given set of feeds and date, and it never touches the recipes: writing a playbook for a new hop stays human work. `composer ci` ends with the offline `--check`: it validates the file's shape against the bundled policy, then recomputes it from the frozen feeds in `tests/fixtures/hop-feeds` as of the file's `generated_on` date, so the check itself needs no network. A scheduled pipeline runs the hop data robot, `bin/hop-data-bot.php`, against the live feeds; when a feed moved while the file slept, the robot opens (or updates) a merge request on Booster itself with the new file, and a person merges it. [MAINTAINING.md](https://github.com/waynestate/booster/blob/main/MAINTAINING.md) covers the token the robot needs.

---

Source: https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/quick-start.html

## Quick start[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/quick-start.html#quick-start)

This page runs Booster on an app for the first time. Next: [What a hop does](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/hops.html) for what each step does.

```
booster detect --path=../my-app        # which of the five permutations, and which versions
booster plan   --path=../my-app        # the ordered hops to a supported version
booster scan   --path=../my-app --php=<target>   # what will break on that newer PHP; advisory, changes nothing
booster run    --path=../my-app --dry-run   # the diffs Rector would make; changes nothing
booster run    --path=../my-app        # apply the plan, one hop at a time, with a test gate
booster init   --path=../my-app        # optional: writes playbooks for AI coding tools into the app; commit them before a real run
```

Replace `<target>` with the PHP version you are heading for, for example the one `plan` shows on its last step.

A real run needs git and Docker on the machine that runs Booster. If you used the Docker-only route, the first four commands above work as they are, but the last one does not: its `php:8.4-cli` image has no git. Use the single-file or clone route for `booster run` (see Install).

Booster prints its progress lines on standard error. In Windows PowerShell they print in red, as if they were errors. They are not errors; the exit code tells you whether the run worked.

### What a run does by default[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/quick-start.html#what-a-run-does-by-default)

You can run `detect`, `plan` and `run` on an app with nothing after `--path`. Booster then goes as far as it safely can on its own: it climbs to the newest PHP and Laravel that CREED's policy supports today, which is PHP 8.5 and Laravel 13 as of this writing (the policy file is the source of truth, not this page).

| Command | With no other flags |
| --- | --- |
| `booster detect` | Reads `composer.json` and `composer.lock`, and reports PHP, Laravel, PHPUnit and the front-end setup. Changes nothing. |
| `booster plan` | Starts from what `detect` found and plans every hop up to the newest PHP, Laravel and PHPUnit the policy supports. Changes nothing. |
| `booster run` | Does the whole plan in one go, in order. |

How many hops? One for every step on the way, never a jump:

- one hop per PHP minor (8.1 to 8.2 is a hop, 8.2 to 8.3 is another),
- one hop per Laravel major,
- one hop per PHPUnit major.

Booster interleaves them so the app sits on a PHP and Laravel pair that Laravel supports at every step: a Laravel step as soon as the current PHP allows it, a PHPUnit step when the PHP allows it, a PHP step otherwise. Two real examples: a Laravel 10 app on PHP 8.1 plans 11 hops, and a PHP 5.5 app with no framework plans 12 hops to PHP 8.5.

Some hops come along by default, and some only when you ask:

- The front-end Node hops (Mix to Vite, Vite major, Tailwind, TypeScript, Vue) are in the plan by default. Pass any target (`--goal`, `--to-php`, `--to-laravel`, `--to-phpunit`, `--from-php`, `--from-laravel`) and they drop out with a warning, unless you add `--with-node`.
- An app on PHPUnit 8 or older gets a manual PHPUnit 9 step before the first PHP 8 hop.
- The SESAME move (`--sesame`) and the WayneUI move (`--wayneui`) are opt-in only.
- `--skip <hop id>` drops a hop you do not want.
- If a target is past security support, the plan stops at the policy limit and warns. If Rector has no ruleset for a step yet, the plan stops short and warns.

`run` handles each hop the same way: a Rector preview, then the edits (if a hop would change more than 200 files it asks first, or stops when it cannot ask; `--max-changes` sets a hard limit), then the Composer constraints, then your tests in the target PHP image. That last part is the gate. The first hop that fails stops the run, and the hops after it are reported as "not run". Booster never commits; the changes sit in your working copy for you to review. Progress prints one line per hop, like `hop 3/11 <hop id>: <status>, 12 files, 41 s`, and ends with `run finished: 11 of 11 hops run, 0 stopped, ...`.

Looking for a specific situation (only PHP, one hop at a time, backend only, a big app, no tests)? See [How do I...](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/recipes.html).

Want less than the whole climb (we will not judge, it is a long way up)?

- `--dry-run` previews every hop and changes nothing.
- `--until <hop id>` keeps that hop and everything before it.
- `--only <hop id>` runs just that one hop.
- `--to-php` and `--to-laravel` pick a lower target.

The one-command form for a forced image upgrade:

```
booster run --path=../my-app --goal=php-74-to-84
```

When the app carries a `composer.lock`, `detect` also reads the PHP range the locked packages allow: the highest `require.php` floor and the lowest ceiling across `packages` and `packages-dev`, raised by a `platform-overrides.php` or `config.platform.php` pin in `composer.json` when one is set. If that floor sits above the floor `composer.json` claims, Booster plans from the lock's floor and prints a warning saying so; if the first PHP hop lands at or above the lock's ceiling, a second warning notes that hop will need a `composer update` to keep the lock installable. Without a lock, `composer.json` stays the sole source.

A plan for the bundled Laravel 10 example app on PHP 8.2 looks like this (the order keeps the app on a PHP and Laravel pair Laravel supports at every step):

```bash
booster plan --path=examples/laravel-blade --today=2026-10-29
```


## The replay gate[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/replay-gate.html#the-replay-gate)

This page shows how to make the gate prove more than the tests do: Booster records how the app answers a list of requests before the upgrade, replays the same requests after every hop, and fails the hop when an answer changes. Before this: [What a hop does](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/hops.html). Next: [Hand-copied libraries to Composer](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/framework-hops.html).

The test gate only knows what the tests ask. Plenty of WSU apps have one smoke test, or none, and the code a PHP hop changes most (string to number comparisons, `null` passed to `strlen`, a dynamic property) sits in pages no test visits. The replay gate takes the patient's vitals before the shot and again after every dose: it writes down what the app said on the old PHP, and after every hop it asks again and compares. It is off unless you ask for it.

### In three commands[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/replay-gate.html#in-three-commands)

```sh
booster replay init --path=<app>           # draft booster-replay.json from the app's routes
# edit booster-replay.json: fill in every "todo", then delete it
booster replay record --path=<app>         # optional: record once and save the answers
booster run --path=<app> --replay          # record, then replay after every hop
```

`booster run --replay` needs nothing else: it records the baseline on the app's current PHP before the first hop (right after the test baseline), so `replay record` is only for when you want to look at the answers first, keep them, or check a hand-made change with `booster replay check --php=8.4`. `--replay=FILE` names another request file; `--replay-out=DIR` picks where the transcripts go.

### What a run does with it[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/replay-gate.html#what-a-run-does-with-it)

1. Before the first hop, Booster serves the untouched app with PHP's built-in server inside `booster-target:<old php>-<stamp>`, the same image the baseline uses, sends every request in the file, and writes the answers to `baseline-php<old>.txt`. The run says so next to the baseline:
   ```
   Replay: recorded 11 answers on PHP 7.4 from booster-replay.json.
   ```
   When a later hop runs the build gate (`vite-major`, `tailwind-3-to-4`, `typescript-major` and the other front-end hops), Booster first runs `npm ci` and `npm run build` in the Node container, so the baseline serves the built front end the hops will rebuild, not a missing or stub `public/build/manifest.json`. If the baseline cannot be recorded (the front end does not build, the setup command failed, the server never answered, an answer missed its `expect`), the upgrade does not start, and nothing is changed.
2. After each hop's tests pass, Booster serves the changed app on the new PHP, sends the same requests, and compares. A match adds `Replay passed: all 11 answers match the baseline from PHP 7.4.` to the hop. A difference fails the hop like a red test, leaves the changes in place, and shows the first difference:
   ```
   Replay failed on PHP 8.0: 1 of 2 answers differ from the baseline from PHP 7.4.
   First difference: 02 requests / a word: GET /compare?code=abc (- baseline, + now)
           "code": "abc",
     -     "matches_zero": true
     +     "matches_zero": false
       }
   Every difference: diff /tmp/booster-replay-notes-20261105-201500/baseline-php7.4.txt /tmp/booster-replay-notes-20261105-201500/step-1-php-74-to-80-php8.0.txt
   ```
   That one is real: `0 == "abc"` is true on PHP 7.4 and false on PHP 8, and no test in the app asked.
3. `--dry-run` sends no requests and says the replay was skipped.

The transcripts are plain text, one block per request, written outside the app (in the temp folder unless `--replay-out` says otherwise), so `diff` and any editor read them. PHP errors and deprecations logged while serving are counted and written next to the transcript (`baseline-php7.4.php-errors.txt`); they are reported, never compared, because a hop is supposed to change them.

### The request file[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/replay-gate.html#the-request-file)

`booster-replay.json` sits in the app's root. Keys that start with `$` are comments. A small one:

```json
{
    "version": 1,
    "serve": {
        "docroot": "public",
        "front_controller": "index.php",
        "setup": "php replay/seed.php",
        "env": { "DB_DATABASE": "/tmp/app.sqlite" },
        "ini": { "date.timezone": "UTC" }
    },
    "normalize": ["csrf", "timestamps"],
    "sequences": [
        {
            "name": "save then read back",
            "requests": [
                { "name": "form", "path": "/", "capture": { "token": "name=\"_token\" value=\"([^\"]+)\"" } },
                { "name": "save", "method": "POST", "path": "/notes",
                  "form": { "_token": "{{token}}", "title": "Replay note" },
                  "capture": { "id": "Location: /notes/(\\d+)" }, "expect": 302 },
                { "name": "read back", "path": "/notes/{{id}}", "expect": 200 }
            ]
        }
    ]
}
```

- **`serve`**: `docroot` (relative, inside the app; default `.`), `front_controller` (a PHP file in the docroot that every path without a file of its own goes to, like Apache's rewrite to `index.php`; leave it out and the server serves the docroot as files), `setup` (a shell command run once, in the app folder, before the server starts: seed a SQLite file, write a `.env`), `env` and `ini` (passed to the setup and the server), and `services`.
- **`requests`** or **`sequences`**: a request has `path`, and may have `name`, `method` (default GET), `query`, `headers`, `cookies`, one body (`form`, `json` or a raw `body`), `capture` and `expect`. A sequence shares a cookie jar, so a session started by one request carries to the next. Redirects are recorded, never followed.
- **`capture`**: a regular expression whose first group is saved under a name, matched against the body and the headers (as `Name: value` lines). Later requests in the same sequence use it as `{{name}}` in the path, query, headers, cookies or body. A placeholder nobody captured is an error when the file loads, not a surprise later.
- **`expect`**: the status the baseline must answer. It is checked while recording only, so a baseline that is already broken (a 500 where a 200 belongs) is refused instead of faithfully recorded.
- **`defaults`**: headers every request gets.
- **`todo`**: a note for a person, on the file, `serve` or a request. `record`, `check` and `run --replay` refuse a file that still has one.

#### What is compared[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/replay-gate.html#what-is-compared)

For each answer: the status, `Content-Type`, `Location` (with the server's own address written as `<app>`), `Allow`, the names of the cookies set (never their values), and the body. Everything else (`Date`, `X-Powered-By`, the values of cookies) changes on every request or every PHP, and is left out. By default runs of spaces and blank lines do not matter, and a JSON body is compared by value, so a reordered key or `1.0` against `1` is not a difference. `"compare": {"whitespace": "exact", "json": "exact"}` compares byte for byte.

#### Normalizers[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/replay-gate.html#normalizers)

A normalizer rewrites the volatile parts of an answer before it is compared and written. The presets:

| Name | Hides |
| --- | --- |
| `csrf` | CSRF tokens in hidden form fields and meta tags (`_token`, `csrf_token`, `authenticity_token` and friends) |
| `session-id` | session ids in links, forms and scripts (`PHPSESSID=...`, `laravel_session=...`) |
| `timestamps` | dates with a time of day, and Unix times from 2020 to 2033 |
| `asset-hash` | content hashes in built asset names (`app.3f9a1c2b.js`, Vite's `app-L1fqnEWe.js`, `app.js?id=3f9a1c`) |
| `preload-hints` | `<link rel="modulepreload">` tags, which list the chunks the bundler split out and change with any build; the tags that load the page stay compared |
| `inertia` | the Inertia page object's asset `version`, the fields Inertia 3 changed (`clearHistory` and `encryptHistory` when false, `sharedProps`) and its devtools id; component, props and url stay compared |

`booster replay init` lists `asset-hash` and `preload-hints` when the app builds with Vite, and `inertia` when it requires `inertiajs/inertia-laravel`. Without them the first front-end hop fails the replay on a sound change: on WELD, `inertia-2-to-3` changed only these parts of every page.

Anything else is an object: `{"name": "request id", "pattern": "req-[0-9a-f]{12}", "replace": "req-<ID>", "in": "body"}`, where `in` is `body` (the default), `headers` or `all`. The patterns are PCRE without delimiters. Normalizers are not part of the recording's fingerprint, so adding one after a failed check does not mean recording again; changing a request does, and `check` says so.

### Design[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/replay-gate.html#design)

- **Served the way the gate already runs.** The app is served by `php -S` inside the same `booster-target` image as the test gate, on the same PHP, with the app folder mounted. No Apache, no nginx, no second image to build. A small router script (shipped with Booster) gives the built-in server the front controller rewrite and leaves real files alone.
- **No network.** The replay container runs with `--network none`; the client talks to the server over the container's own loopback. A request that tries to reach a real database, CAS or an API fails the same way on both sides of the hop, instead of touching anything real. When the app needs a database server, `serve.services` starts fixture containers (`{"name": "db", "image": "mysql:8.4", "env": {...}}`) on a private Docker network created with `--internal`, reachable by name, removed afterwards. Fake data only.
- **Composer runs where the network is.** A standalone `replay record` or `check` runs `composer install` in a normal gate container first (`--no-install` skips it); inside `booster run` the test gate has already installed `vendor/`.
- **Old PHP included.** The client and router are written for PHP 5.5 and up, because the baseline of an app on PHP 5.6 runs inside a PHP 5.6 image. A test holds them to it.
- **Fail closed.** No baseline, no upgrade. A recording made from a different request file is refused. A request that got no answer is a difference, not a pass.
- **Nothing written into the app.** The setup command may write where the app's own settings point (`/tmp` is good); Booster's scratch files live in a temp folder it mounts and removes. `booster replay record` saves `booster-replay.recording.json` in the app because you asked it to keep the answers; commit it or ignore it.

### Drafting the file[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/replay-gate.html#drafting-the-file)

`booster replay init` writes a first draft and never overwrites one. It looks, in order, for:

1. `php artisan route:list --json`, when the app is Laravel and `vendor/` is installed (otherwise the `Route::` calls in `routes/`);
2. Slim-style route calls (`$app->get('/batches/:id', ...)`), the kind a legacy Slim 1 app has in its `index.php`;
3. PHP entry points under the docroot, skipping include folders, with a POST draft for each page that reads `$_POST`.

Every GET without parameters becomes a request, plus one unknown path (an honest 404 is an answer too). Every path parameter, form and setup command gets a `todo`, because Booster cannot know which note id exists or what a valid form looks like. Fill those in, delete the `todo` lines, and record.

### Limits, honestly[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/replay-gate.html#limits-honestly)

- **No real Oracle, SSO or CAS.** The replay never reaches a real system, by design. An app that cannot render a page without Oracle needs a fake for that page (an environment switch to SQLite, a stub repository), or that page stays out of the file. Pages behind CAS or Entra need the app's own test login (a fake user in the session, the way its tests sign in); without one, the honest request is the guest's: the redirect to sign-in.
- **No JavaScript.** The client speaks HTTP, like curl. A page that builds itself in the browser is compared as the HTML and JSON the server sends, which still catches a changed API answer, but not a broken click.
- **One server, one process.** `php -S` is not Apache: `.htaccess` rules other than the front controller rewrite, `mod_php` settings and server-side includes do not apply. Put the PHP settings that matter in `serve.ini`.
- **The same data on both sides.** The setup command runs again before every replay, so each side starts from the same fixture. An app that keeps state elsewhere (a file cache under `storage/`, a queue) can answer differently for reasons that are not the hop; clear it in `setup`.
- **Time, randomness and order.** Normalizers cover the common volatile parts. Anything else the app makes up per request (a request id, a shuffled list) needs a custom normalizer or a fixed seed in `setup`.
- **Answers, not side effects.** The gate compares what the app says, not what it wrote to a database or a mail queue. A follow-up request that reads the saved record back (like `read back` above) covers the common case.

---

Source: https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/scans.html

## The scans[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/scans.html#the-scans)

This page covers both advisory scans Booster runs with `plan`, and how to run either one alone. Next: [The dependency check](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/dependency-check.html).

### The PHPCompatibility scan[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/scans.html#the-phpcompatibility-scan)

`plan` ends with an advisory scan: PHP_CodeSniffer runs the PHPCompatibility standard over the app and asks what will break on the PHP version the first PHP hop lands on. The findings are hints for the person doing the upgrade, never a gate: they do not change the exit code, and a scan that cannot run (missing tooling, a crash) is reported as "could not run" while the plan still prints in full. `--no-scan` skips both advisory scans.

The scan needs no change to the app: Booster ships PHP_CodeSniffer and the PHPCompatibility standard with its own dependencies, from the PHAR and from a clone alike. Booster looks for a PHP_CodeSniffer that carries the standard, trying the app's own `vendor/bin/phpcs`, then Booster's `vendor/bin/phpcs`, then `phpcs` on the PATH. When it runs Booster's own copy, it points PHP_CodeSniffer at the bundled standard with `--runtime-set installed_paths`, because the registration file that Composer's installer plugin writes cannot be trusted inside a PHAR unpacked into a temp directory. When none of the launchers has the standard, the scan reports a skip and the plan goes on; the skip says to reinstall Booster's dependencies (`composer install` in Booster's folder) or download the PHAR again.

The scan ignores `vendor/`, `node_modules/` and `storage/`, because those hold third-party code and generated files, not the app's. It reads the app only and changes nothing. `booster scan --path=../my-app --php=<target>` runs the same scan on its own, for any PHP version Booster knows, and exits 0 even when it finds a wall of removed functions. If the app's `composer.json` declares `ext-oci8` (in `require`, `require-dev` or `config.platform`), the scan leaves out the "`oci_*()` is removed since PHP 8.4" findings: PHP 8.4 moved oci8 out of the PHP download and into PECL, and an app that declares the extension installs the PECL one on purpose, so those lines would be false alarms. Every other finding stays.

### The PHPStan scan[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/scans.html#the-phpstan-scan)

`plan` ends with a second advisory scan: PHPStan runs over the app at the destination PHP version, using Pinstripe's `base.neon` preset. The findings are hints for the person doing the upgrade, never a gate: they do not change the exit code, and a scan that cannot run is reported with the fix that enables it, while the plan still prints in full. `--no-scan` skips it.

The scan needs no change to the app: Booster ships PHPStan and Pinstripe's preset with its own dependencies, from the PHAR and from a clone alike. Booster looks for a PHPStan binary, trying the app's own `vendor/bin/phpstan`, then Booster's `vendor/bin/phpstan`, then `phpstan` on the PATH, and for the preset it tries the app's vendor tree and Booster's. When either is missing, the report says to reinstall Booster's dependencies (`composer install` in Booster's folder) or download the PHAR again.

It ignores `vendor/`, `node_modules/` and `storage/`, reads the app only and changes nothing. `booster scan --path=../my-app --php=8.5 --phpstan` runs the same scan on its own, for any PHP version Booster knows, and exits 0 even when it finds a wall of missing types.

### The composer audit during the run[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/scans.html#the-composer-audit-during-the-run)

`run` carries a third advisory check, per hop: after a hop changes `composer.json` or `composer.lock`, Booster runs `composer audit --format=json --no-interaction` in the app and lists advisories and abandoned packages in the step's report with counts. It never changes the exit code, a clean audit stays silent, and a hop that changed no composer file skips it and says so. A dry run previews the hops and runs no audit.

---

Source: https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/smoke-test.html

## A smoke test for WSU apps[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/smoke-test.html#a-smoke-test-for-wsu-apps)

This page shows the one small test that gives the gate something real to prove. Next: [What a hop does](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/hops.html).

Laravel's stock tests do not fit a WSU app. `tests/Feature/ExampleTest.php` asks for `/` and expects 200, but on a real app the front page sits behind CAS, so an unauthenticated request is a redirect to the sign-in URL, never a 200. The stock suite also assumes an `APP_URL` that points somewhere real and an `APP_KEY` that exists; a fresh checkout has neither, so the suite is red before any change, and even a green run of it proves nothing about the upgrade. When Booster sees only the two stock example tests, it says so next to the baseline:

```
The app's tests are only Laravel's stock examples, so the gate cannot prove anything. See "A smoke test for WSU apps" in the README.
```

Write one small test that proves the app boots and its front door still works. It needs a few environment values in `phpunit.xml`, because the test environment starts empty:

```xml
<php>
    <env name="APP_ENV" value="testing"/>
    <env name="APP_KEY" value="base64:c21va2UtdGVzdC1rZXkwMDAwMDAwMDAwMDAwMDAwMDA="/>
    <env name="APP_URL" value="http://localhost"/>
</php>
```

`APP_KEY` can be any throwaway 32-byte key (`php artisan key:generate --show`); it never leaves the test environment. If the app touches the database while booting, point the tests at an in-memory SQLite database:

```xml
    <env name="DB_CONNECTION" value="sqlite"/>
    <env name="DB_DATABASE" value=":memory:"/>
```

And the test itself, in `tests/Feature/SmokeTest.php`:

```php
<?php

namespace Tests\Feature;

use Tests\TestCase;

final class SmokeTest extends TestCase
{
    public function test_a_guest_is_sent_to_the_cas_login(): void
    {
        $response = $this->get('/');

        $response->assertRedirect();
        $this->assertStringContainsString('/login', (string) $response->headers->get('Location'));
    }
}
```

That is the whole point: the app boots, encryption and sessions work, and the front door still sends guests to CAS. It passes on the old PHP and must still pass on the new one, which is what the gate is for.

Those values live in `phpunit.xml`, committed with the app. When you would rather not commit them, pass them on the command line instead; Booster forwards each one to the baseline and every gate container with `-e`, and the report names the keys only, never the values:

```
booster run --path=<app> --test-env DB_CONNECTION=sqlite --test-env DB_DATABASE=:memory:
```

---

Source: https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/

## Booster[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/#booster)

This page says what Booster is and where to go next. Install it on [Install](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/install.html), then follow [Quick start](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/quick-start.html).

**Boosts your versions.** One dose at a time, and every dose gets a stamp.

> A booster shot keeps your immunity current. This one keeps your PHP current, and it stings less.

Booster is WELD's upgrade tool. It plans the hops that take a WSU PHP app from the PHP or Laravel version it runs now to one the version policy still supports, and it runs them one at a time: [Rector](https://getrector.com) rewrites the code, Booster raises the constraints in `composer.json`, and the app's own tests must pass on the target PHP before the next hop starts. It stands on `rector/rector` and `driftingly/rector-laravel` and adds only the ordering, the review threshold, the gate, the advisory scans and a few WSU recipes.

Booster edits your working copy and prints a report. It never commits to, pushes or opens a merge request on your app (the only merge requests it opens are its own hop-data refresh on Booster itself): a person reads the diff and merges it.

**Not to be confused with:** Booster moves an app to a newer PHP or framework version; Pinstripe's Rector set only modernizes code within the PHP version the app already runs.

### Where it fits in WELD[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/#where-it-fits-in-weld)

WELD is the Wayne State application stack. Booster is its upgrade layer.

| Part | Job |
| --- | --- |
| WayneUI (project 0) | The interface layer every other part builds on |
| CREED | The version policy (`policy.json`) Booster reads |
| PROCTOR | Measures an app against that policy; the gate runs it before the first hop and after the last |
| Preflight | The CI templates |
| SESAME | Auth; Booster can swap `wayne-cas` for it |
| HELMET | The baseline runtime |
| Pinstripe | The coding standard |
| Sourdough | The starters |
| Booster | This project: moves apps forward |

It works for all five permutations of the stack: raw PHP, raw PHP with a Vue SPA, Laravel with Blade, Laravel with Blade and Vue islands, and Laravel with Inertia and Vue.

### Run it today[#](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/#run-it-today)

Two one-liners get Booster onto your machine:

```
curl -L -o ~/bin/booster.phar https://github.com/waynestate/booster/releases/latest/download/booster.phar
```

or, from Packagist:

```
composer create-project waynestate/booster booster ^1.0
```

Then the first command, run from inside the app you want to upgrade:

```bash
booster detect
```

```output
path           .
app_type       laravel-blade
composer_json  yes
php            8.2
laravel        10
phpunit        10
vue            unknown
node           unknown
mix_file       no
wayne_cas      no
wayneui_1      no
boost          no
helmet         no

Nothing was changed. This is what Booster read from composer.json and package.json; "php" is the lowest PHP version
composer.json allows, not what your server runs (if it is wrong, add --from-php=X.Y to plan).
Keys: composer_json = composer.json found, mix_file = webpack.mix.js found, wayne_cas = the cit-web-infra/wayne-cas package, wayneui_1 = the cit-web-infra/wayne-ui package, boost = the laravel/boost package, helmet = the waynestate/helmet package.
Next: php bin/booster plan --path=.
```

Every route, per OS, is on [Install](https://booster.apps.wayne.edu/docs/install.html).
